html:
Sugarcane is a tall tropical grass with thick, sweet stalks, the source of most of the world's sugar. It was first tamed in New Guinea, where early farmers grew it thousands of years ago, and it spread with Austronesian sailors across the Pacific and Southeast Asia to India.

In India people learned to boil cane juice down into solid sugar, and later into crystals; see crystal sugar. Persians and then Arabs took the plant west, and in the Arab agricultural revolution it was grown with irrigation in Egypt, Sicily and Spain. Sugar stayed a luxury.

Cane is hard work: it must be cut and crushed fast and boiled in hot mills. In the 1400s the Portuguese and Spanish grew it on Atlantic islands with enslaved labour. Then they took it to the Americas, and sugar became the engine of the Atlantic slave trade:

  • In the 1500s Brazil led, with mills around Salvador da Bahia and Pernambuco. Runaways from these estates built Palmares.
  • In the 1600s and 1700s the Caribbean islands took over. Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, was the richest sugar colony of all, and the islands' molasses gave rum.
  • In the 1800s Cuba, worked from Havana, became the great producer.

Millions of Africans were shipped to grow it. After slavery ended, planters brought indentured workers from India, China and the Pacific islands. In Australia, cane toads were released in 1935 to eat cane beetles, and became a pest themselves.
